name: __elfN(imgact)
prose: __elfN(imgact)(imgp) treats imgp->image_header as an ELF header; the caller holds imgp->vp locked shared. It returns -1 (line 1044, before anything is changed) if __elfN(check_header) fails or e_type is neither ET_EXEC nor ET_DYN. Past that point it returns an errno or 0. Two ENOEXEC returns leave without going through the cleanup label: e_phoff + e_phnum*e_phentsize wraps, and e_phnum exceeds __elfN(phnums); nothing has been allocated or changed at that point. Every other exit goes to label ret, which asserts that imgp->vp is locked, frees interp if it was allocated by __elfN(get_interp) (free_interp), frees the temporary program-header buffer m_phdrs (NULL when the headers were read from the header page) and returns error. Errors reaching ret: an error from vn_rdwr reading the program headers (the vnode is unlocked during the malloc and relocked shared before the read); ENOEXEC for a PT_LOAD alignment that is not a power of two or exceeds the maximum, for a mapsize overflow, for a second PT_INTERP, and for a PT_GNU_STACK whose translated protection lacks read and write (checked only when __elfN(nxstack) is set); the error from __elfN(get_interp); ENOEXEC when __elfN(get_brandinfo) returns NULL; ENOEXEC for an ET_DYN file whose brand lacks BI_CAN_EXEC_DYN; ENOEXEC for 'Excessive mapping size' (mapsz >= maxv - vm_map_min); under PAX_ASLR ENOEXEC for a non-ET_DYN file when can_exec_nonpie fails; and any error from __elfN(load_sections), __elfN(enforce_limits), __elfN(load_interp) or exec_map_stack. Side effects before the later checks: when imgp->credential_setid is set it clears the ASLR and WXORX bits in p_flag2 under the proc lock; once the brand is chosen it calls exec_new_vmspace and then stores sv in imgp->proc->p_sysent and brand_info in p_elf_brandinfo before testing the result of exec_new_vmspace (an error from it is kept in error and is replaced by ENOEXEC if the mapping-size check also fails), so these fields and the new vmspace can be left in place when an error is returned. PT_GNU_STACK sets imgp->stack_sz, and imgp->stack_prot only when __elfN(nxstack) is set. On success it returns 0 after setting imgp->entry_addr, anon_loc of the new map, imgp->auxargs (a freshly allocated Elf_Auxargs), imgp->interpreted = 0, imgp->reloc_base, p_osrel, p_fctl0 and p_elf_flags; imgp->et_dyn_addr is set to ET_DYN_LOAD_ADDR (or the PAX ASLR base) for an ET_DYN file with a zero first load address.
note: slice cut the head (starts at line 1034 inside the body); real function is the static ELF activator defined with the __elfN macro name. Old prose said 'returns 0 ... or errno' without the early-return split and wrongly implied no state change on failure after exec_new_vmspace; rewritten from returns list at imgact_elf.c lines 1044,1063,1068,1083 and ret at 1323-1328.

name: __elfN(trans_prot)
prose: __elfN(trans_prot)(flags) returns a vm_prot_t built from flags with a single return at the end: VM_PROT_EXECUTE is set when PF_X is set in flags, VM_PROT_WRITE when PF_W is set, VM_PROT_READ when PF_R is set, and no other bit is set in the result; bits of flags other than PF_X, PF_W and PF_R are ignored. It reads and writes no global state and takes no locks.
note: slice began inside the body/included untrans_prot; real function is the static trans_prot defined with the __elfN macro name (imgact_elf.c 2835-2848). Old prose correct apart from 'Generated function' wording; no lock or memory effect.

name: vty_enabled
prose: vty_enabled(vty) uses the static variable vty_selected (initially 0) and the static buffer vty_name. If vty_selected is still 0 it fetches the tunable kern.vty into vty_name with TUNABLE_STR_FETCH, then picks the console driver: with DEV_SC compiled in and vty_name equal to 'sc' it selects VTY_SC; with DEV_VT compiled in and vty_name equal to 'vt' it selects VTY_VT; otherwise it defaults to VTY_VT if DEV_VT is compiled in, else to VTY_SC if DEV_SC is compiled in (if neither is compiled in, vty_selected stays 0). When vty_selected is then VTY_VT or VTY_SC it overwrites vty_name with 'vt' or 'sc'. There is a single return, which returns whether (vty_selected & vty) is non-zero. When vty_selected is already non-zero, the selection is not redone. No lock is taken, so concurrent first calls can both run the selection.
note: slice cut the head (starts at line 772 inside vty_enabled, kern_cons.c 745-778); old prose wrongly described vty_name as a caller buffer and a parameter. vty_name is a static 16-byte file-scope buffer; function takes only 'unsigned vty'.

name: cf_set_method
prose: cf_set_method(dev, level, priority) changes the CPU frequency level of dev's cpufreq softc. It first calls the cpufreq_pre_change event handlers with level and &error; if they set error non-zero it calls the cpufreq_post_change handlers with level and that error and returns that error without taking sc->lock. Otherwise it takes sc->lock (CF_MTX_LOCK) and every later path goes through label out, which drops sc->lock, calls the cpufreq_post_change handlers with level and error, prints 'set freq failed' when error is non-zero and the local pointer set is non-NULL, and returns error. Paths to out: ENXIO when SMP is configured without EARLY_AP_STARTUP, mp_ncpus > 1 and smp_started is not yet set; EPERM when priority is lower than sc->curr_priority; when level is NULL, ENXIO if sc->saved_freq is empty, otherwise the first saved entry's level and priority are used instead; EINVAL if level->total_set.freq is below cf_lowest_freq; ENXIO if the absolute-setting device (set->dev non-NULL) or any relative-setting device is not attached; error 0 with no level recorded when the absolute-setting device's CPU has no pcpu (cpu_get_pcpu returns NULL); an error from CPUFREQ_DRV_SET for the absolute or any relative setting (earlier settings are not backed out); and ENOMEM if the malloc (M_NOWAIT) that saves the previous level fails. If the requested frequency equals sc->curr_level.total_set.freq the driver calls are skipped, but the code still continues to the 'skip' step below, so this case can also return ENOMEM. At the skip step, if the current frequency is not CPUFREQ_VAL_UNKNOWN and priority is higher than sc->curr_priority, the current level and priority are pushed onto sc->saved_freq. Then sc->curr_level = *level and sc->curr_priority = priority are recorded; if a saved level was being restored, sc->curr_level.total_set.freq is set to CPUFREQ_VAL_UNKNOWN, the saved entry is removed from sc->saved_freq and freed, and the post-change handlers are then called with a level pointer that referred to that freed entry. It returns 0 on those completed paths unless an error was set above. During each driver call the thread is temporarily bound to the target CPU at priority PRI_MIN and restored afterwards.
note: slice cut the head: the function is cf_set_method(device_t dev, const struct cf_level *level, int priority) (kern_cpu.c 238-426), not cpufreq_set. Reviewer claim (already-current path can return ENOMEM) is right: the goto skip at line 321 falls into the save-previous-level malloc (394-398) which can set ENOMEM.

name: kern_cpuset_getdomain
prose: kern_cpuset_getdomain(td, level, which, id, domainsetsize, maskp, policyp, cb) returns ERANGE if domainsetsize is below sizeof(domainset_t) or above DOMAINSET_MAXSIZE / NBBY, and otherwise the error from cpuset_check_capabilities if that is non-zero; both of these return before anything is allocated. It then allocates a zeroed temporary mask of domainsetsize bytes and calls cpuset_which2, whose error (for example ESRCH or EPERM) is returned after freeing the buffer. Under CPU_LEVEL_ROOT or CPU_LEVEL_CPUSET it takes the thread's cpuset (CPU_WHICH_TID, CPU_WHICH_PID) or the set found by cpuset_which2 (CPU_WHICH_CPUSET, CPU_WHICH_JAIL), takes the root or base set of it and copies its domainset to a local outset; the CPU_WHICH_IRQ, INTRHANDLER, ITHREAD and DOMAIN selections give EINVAL. Under CPU_LEVEL_WHICH it copies the thread's domainset (TID), ORs the masks of all threads in the process and takes the policy and preferred domain of the last thread (PID), or copies the cpuset's domainset (CPUSET, JAIL); the other selections give EINVAL; any other level gives EINVAL. It then releases the cpuset reference if one was held and drops the proc lock if one was held, and if outset.ds_policy is DOMAINSET_POLICY_PREFER it replaces the mask with a mask holding only ds_prefer. If error is still 0 it copies the mask out with cb->cpuset_copyout(mask, maskp, domainsetsize) and returns that callback's error if non-zero; then it stores the policy with suword32 and sets EFAULT if that fails. The temporary mask is freed on every path that allocated it and the function returns error; 0 only when both copy-outs succeeded.
note: Both reviewer claims are right: the size and capability checks are returns of the function (kern_cpuset.c 2297-2302), not preconditions. The 'every path releases references' claim is true on my reading (goto out at 2307 and 2326 occur only when p and set are NULL), but the old prose said EFAULT for the copyout, which is whatever cb->cpuset_copyout returns.

name: cpuset_modify_domain
prose: cpuset_modify_domain(set, domain) is static. It returns the error of priv_check(curthread, PRIV_SCHED_CPUSET) if non-zero, and EPERM if the current credential is jailed and set has CPU_SET_ROOT; both returns happen before any allocation or lock. Otherwise it initialises a freelist of domainsets, replaces domain by the result of domainset_create(domain), and takes the spin lock cpuset_lock. In a loop it gets the root of set and returns EINVAL (via out) if domainset_valid(root's domainset, domain) fails; if the policy is DOMAINSET_POLICY_PREFER it copies set->cs_domain's current mask into domain->ds_mask; it then calls cpuset_testupdate_domain, going to out with its error if non-zero. If the number of free domainsets already prepared is at least the number needed it leaves the loop; otherwise it drops the spin lock, adds the missing entries to the freelist, retakes the lock and re-evaluates. After the loop it calls cpuset_update_domain on set, which applies the domainset to set and its descendants. At out it releases cpuset_lock, frees the leftover freelist entries, and calls domainset_notify() only when error is 0. It returns 0 on success; on the error paths from out nothing has been applied to the hierarchy because the update is only reached after the validity and testupdate checks succeeded.
note: Reviewer claim (privilege/jail are checks, not preconditions) is right; the old prose already listed them as returns, so it was kept in substance and the preconditions wording and an unqualified 'on every error path' removed (kern_cpuset.c 812-883).

name: kern_dup
prose: kern_dup(td, mode, flags, old, new) duplicates descriptor old to a new descriptor in the calling process's table. Returns before taking the table lock: EBADF if old < 0; if new < 0, or new >= getmaxfd(td), EINVAL when mode is FDDUP_FCNTL and EBADF otherwise. It then takes the filedesc exclusive lock. Returns EBADF (lock released) if descriptor old is not open (fget_noref returns NULL) or if fhold on its file fails. If mode is FDDUP_FIXED and old == new it sets td->td_retval[0] = new, ORs fddup_to_fde_flags(flags) into that entry's flags, releases the lock and returns 0 without taking a new reference. Otherwise it takes a reference on the old file with fhold and obtains the target: for FDDUP_NORMAL and FDDUP_FCNTL it calls fdalloc(td, new, &new), and on error drops the reference, releases the lock and returns that error; new may then be a different (higher) descriptor number than requested; for FDDUP_FIXED, if new >= fd_nfiles it (under RACCT, when enabled) calls racct_set_unlocked(p, RACCT_NOFILE, new + 1) and on failure drops the reference, releases the lock and returns EMFILE, then grows the table to new + 1, and it marks new used if it was not. It then copies the file pointer and capabilities from the old entry to the new entry (sequence-count write bracket under CAPABILITIES), sets the new entry's flags to the old flags without UF_EXCLOSE and UF_FOCLOSE ORed with fddup_to_fde_flags(flags), sets td->td_retval[0] = new and error = 0. If the new entry previously held a file (delfp, only possible in FDDUP_FIXED mode) it calls closefp on that file, which is entered with the lock held and releases it, and the return value of closefp is ignored; otherwise it releases the lock. It finally frees the old capability ioctl list that was detached from the new entry (filecaps_free_finish) and returns error (0 on the success paths).
note: slice cut the head; the function is kern_dup(td, mode, flags, old, new) (kern_descrip.c 1043-1176), not fddup. The old prose used the wrong name and described fhold/getmaxfd correctly in places but wrongly said 'always releases the table lock via closefp or unlock' without noting that closefp does the unlock, and omitted the old==new FIXED case and the fhold-failure EBADF.

name: do_execve
prose: do_execve(td, args, mac_p, oldvmspace) is the in-kernel implementation of execve/fexecve for thread td; all arguments are consumed (exec_free_args(args) is called on every path that reaches the common exit). It takes the proc lock, waits via execve_block_pass if exec is blocked, sets P_INEXEC and drops the lock; it zeroes a local image_params, records the old credential, p_osrel, p_fctl0 and p_elf_brandinfo, and (with MAC) calls mac_execve_enter, going to exec_fail on error. At label interpret it obtains the image vnode in one of three ways: by name through namei (returning to exec_fail with its error, or ECAPMODE when in capability mode), from an interpreter vnode already supplied by an activator, or from args->fd through fgetvp_exec (error to exec_fail). It then runs exec_check_permissions, PAX checks when configured, maps the first page (exec_map_first_page), clears p_osrel, p_fctl0 and p_elf_brandinfo, decides whether the credentials change (set-id files, not under MNT_NOSUID, not capability mode, not P_TRACED) and builds imgp->newcred, then calls each non-NULL ex_imgact in turn until one returns something other than -1. Failures up to this point jump to exec_fail_dealloc with error set; if no activator matched error becomes ENOEXEC. If the activator set imgp->interpreted, the first page and text reference are released, the old vnode and name are freed and the loop restarts at interpret with the interpreter name. Otherwise it unlocks the vnode and fails with ENOEXEC if disallow_high_osrel rejects the osrel, with the error from sv_copyout_strings, with EINVAL if argc is not positive, with the error from sv_fixup, or with the error from fdcheckstd (set-id case); each of those relocks the vnode and goes to exec_fail_dealloc. On the success path it unshares the file descriptor table and process-descriptor state, closes close-on-exec files, optionally builds a new cached argument copy, copies shared sigacts, then under the proc lock resets signals, names the process and thread, sets P_EXEC, wakes a vfork parent, installs the new credentials (proc_set_cred, freeing the old credential reference), swaps in the new p_textvp, p_textdvp and p_binname, clears P_INEXEC, installs the new argument cache, runs the hwpmc/hwt hooks when active, calls sv_setregs and updates the access time. At exec_fail_dealloc, if error is non-zero it restores the saved p_osrel, p_fctl0 and p_elf_brandinfo; it unmaps the first page, closes and releases the vnode (vput on error, plain unlock on success) and frees the name buffer, deallocates imgp->object and frees the resolved path; on success it sets TDB_EXEC when PTRACE_EXEC is requested, on error (and for jumps to exec_fail) it clears P_INEXEC under the proc lock. It then frees the new credential if it was not installed, the old text vnodes, binname, argument cache, sigacts and uidinfo. If error is non-zero and the vmspace was already destroyed (imgp->vmspace_destroyed) it calls exec_cleanup and kern_exit(td, 0, SIGABRT) instead of returning an error to the caller. Otherwise it returns EJUSTRETURN when error is 0 and error when it is non-zero.
note: slice cut the head and was only a middle fragment; the function is the static do_execve(td, args, mac_p, oldvmspace) (kern_exec.c 457-1179). Old prose was only a fragment and falsely implied an 'imgp is zeroed by the caller' precondition (the function does bzero(imgp) itself at 519).

name: fork1
prose: fork1(td, fr) creates a child process (or, without RFPROC, only unshares resources). It first returns immediately, with no allocations made and without the pause below: the error from pax_segvguard_check when PAX_SEGVGUARD is configured and the process is not pid 0; EINVAL for undefined flags, RFTSIGFLAGS without RFTSIGZMB, RFFDG together with RFCFDG, an out-of-range RFTSIGZMB signal, or RFPROCDESC without RFPROC, without fr_pd_fd or with pd flags outside PD_ALLOWED_AT_FORK. (MPASS checks on fr_procp/fr_pidp are assertions only.) If RFPROC is clear it stores NULL in *fr_procp or, otherwise if fr_pidp is set, 0 in *fr_pidp, and returns fork_norfproc(td, flags). Otherwise it increments nprocs and fails with EAGAIN if the count reaches maxproc - 10 and the caller lacks PRIV_MAXPROC, or reaches maxproc. If p1 has several threads it takes pg_killsx shared, or single-threads the process with thread_single(SINGLE_BOUNDARY) and returns ERESTART if that fails; it returns ERESTART if sx_slock_sig fails, or if the process changed process group or sig_intr() reports a pending signal. It then, if requested, allocates the process descriptor with procdesc_falloc (its error is returned), allocates a proc and thread (ENOMEM if thread_alloc fails; error from thread_recycle), forks the vmspace when RFMEM is clear (ENOMEM if vmspace_fork or swap_reserve fails), copies the credential, and calls racct_proc_fork (EAGAIN on failure), and checks the per-uid process count with chgproccnt (EAGAIN if over the limit without PRIV_PROC_LIMIT). On success it calls do_fork and returns 0 with nprocs left incremented. Every failure after nprocs was incremented goes through fail0/fail1/fail2: it frees the vmspace if any, drops the reference on the new proc, closes and drops the procdesc file if one was allocated, decrements nprocs, then at cleanup releases pg_killsx and ends single-threading if they were taken, and for any non-zero error sleeps hz/2 ticks with pause() before returning the error.
note: slice cut the head (fork1 is at kern_fork.c 896-1171). Reviewer claim 'pause only for EAGAIN' is WRONG: label cleanup runs pause('fork', hz/2) for any non-zero error that reaches it (kern_fork.c 1168-1169). But the old prose was wrong elsewhere: the EINVAL/segvguard/flag-check returns (920-958) return immediately with no cleanup and no pause, racct_proc_fork failure is mapped to EAGAIN (1118), and the failed-limit paths give EAGAIN or ERESTART.

name: kern_jail_set
prose: kern_jail_set(td, optuio, flags) creates and/or updates a jail from the name/value options in optuio. It returns immediately (no cleanup needed) with EPERM if JAIL_CREATE is set without JAIL_AT_DESC and the caller's prison has pr_childmax 0, and with EINVAL if flags contain bits outside JAIL_SET_MASK or both JAIL_USE_DESC and JAIL_AT_DESC. With JAIL_ATTACH it then calls prison_attach_thread_single and returns its error if non-zero. From then on it holds a reference on the caller's prison and every exit goes through the done_deref / done_errmsg / done_free labels. It builds the option list with vfs_buildopts, parses and validates the parameters (desc, jid, securelevel, children.max, enforce_statfs, name, host.*, path, ip4/ip6 addresses, allow and boolean flags and others) and fails with errors that include EINVAL, ENAMETOOLONG, EPERM (when PRIV_JAIL_SET or PRIV_JAIL_ATTACH is denied, or a parent/permission check fails), ENOTDIR and errors from namei or the descriptor helpers (jaildesc_find, jaildesc_alloc). Then it takes the allprison lock exclusively and, depending on jid/name and the CREATE/UPDATE flags, finds or creates the prison, failing with errors that include EAGAIN, EEXIST, ENOENT, EINVAL, EPERM, EADDRINUSE and ENOMEM-type allocation errors. It applies the settings under the prison mutex, calls the OSD methods PR_METHOD_CREATE (for a new jail) and PR_METHOD_SET (errors go to done_deref), marks a new prison alive, attaches the calling process with do_jail_attach if JAIL_ATTACH is set (error becomes 'attach failed'), writes the jail descriptor number back into the 'desc' option if one was requested, and on success sets td->td_retval[0] to the prison id and returns 0. At done_deref it queues NOTE_JAIL_SET for an existing, possibly changed jail, calls prison_deref (or drops the allprison lock itself) and releases the root vnode; for a non-zero error it copies any 'errmsg' text back to the user; at done_free it frees the copied IP lists, drops the descriptor file reference and closes the new descriptor if an error occurred, frees the path buffer and the option list, drops the reference on the caller's prison, ends the attach single-threading when JAIL_ATTACH was set, and returns error. Because settings are applied before later steps can fail, a non-zero return does not guarantee that the jail was left unchanged.
note: slice cut the head and is a middle fragment of kern_jail_set(td, optuio, flags) (kern_jail.c 1006-2372); jail_set is not a separate function. Old prose claimed that failures never create or update a jail, which is false: the code itself notes (2320-2324) that changes may have been made before a failure.

name: trace_cmp
prose: trace_cmp(type, arg1, arg2, ret) is a static comparison-trace hook. It returns false, writing nothing, if get_kinfo(curthread) returns NULL (thread NULL, in an interrupt or with an interrupt frame, no td_kcov_info, or its state is not KCOV_STATE_RUNNING), or if the info's mode is not KCOV_MODE_TRACE_CMP, or if index * 4 + 4 + 1 > info->entries where index is the value read from buf[0] (kvaddr must be non-NULL, which is only a KASSERT). Otherwise it loops: it stores type, arg1, arg2 and ret at buf[index*4+1] through buf[index*4+4], then tries atomic_cmpset_64(&buf[0], index, index + 1); on failure it stores index back into buf[0] and repeats with the same index and no new bounds check. When the compare-and-set succeeds it returns true. It takes no locks and does not allocate or free memory.
note: Reviewer claim is WRONG: after a failed atomic_cmpset_64 the code only executes buf[0] = index and loops again with the same local index (kern_kcov.c 257-259); it does not reload index or recheck the bounds, and the loop has no return false. Old prose matches the code; only the tail was tightened (kern_kcov.c 222-263).

name: __lockmgr_args
prose: __lockmgr_args(lk, flags, ilk, wmesg, pri, timo, file, line) is the generic entry point for lockmgr operations. It returns 0 immediately if SCHEDULER_STOPPED(). It selects the operation op = flags & LK_TYPE_MASK and resolves default wait message, priority and timeout. On a lock created with LK_NOSHARE a shared request is turned into an exclusive one, and an upgrade, try-upgrade or downgrade request just asserts that the lock is exclusively held and not recursed, releases ilk if LK_INTERLOCK was given, and returns 0. For LK_SHARED it returns lockmgr_slock_hard(...); for LK_UPGRADE and LK_TRYUPGRADE lockmgr_upgrade(...); for LK_EXCLUSIVE lockmgr_xlock_hard(...); for LK_RELEASE lockmgr_sunlock_hard(...) when the lock word has LK_SHARE set, otherwise lockmgr_xunlock_hard(...). Each of these returns directly, so the interlock handling for those operations is done by the callee. For LK_DOWNGRADE it asserts exclusive ownership, panics (after releasing ilk if given) if the lock is recursed, then spins on atomic_cmpset_rel_ptr until the exclusive owner word is replaced by one shared holder keeping the waiter flags; it then falls to the common exit. For LK_DRAIN it panics if the caller already holds the lock exclusively; otherwise it loops until it acquires the lock by swapping LK_UNLOCKED to the thread id; if LK_TRYOP(flags) is true and the lock cannot be taken it sets error = EBUSY and leaves the loop; otherwise it takes the sleepqueue chain lock, wakes the exclusive or shared queue when only waiter flags remain, sets LK_EXCLUSIVE_WAITERS, unlocks ilk if it is still held (clearing LK_INTERLOCK), and sleeps on the exclusive queue with sleepq_wait before retrying. On a successful drain it updates lock profiling and witness state and increments the thread's lock count. An unknown op panics. At the common exit it releases ilk if LK_INTERLOCK is still set in flags and returns error, which is 0 except for the EBUSY case of LK_DRAIN with a try flag.
note: slice is the tail of __lockmgr_args(lk, flags, ilk, wmesg, pri, timo, file, line) (kern_lock.c 1287-1592); there is no function named _lockmgr in the file. The slice also contains _lockmgr_disown, lockmgr_printinfo, _lockmgr_assert and lockmgr_chain, which are other functions and are not described here.

name: lf_setlock
prose: lf_setlock(state, lock, vp, cookiep) (static) tries to set the byte-range lock described by lock on the file state. It first computes the sleep priority (PLOCK, plus 4 for F_WRLCK, with PCATCH unless F_NOINTR). If lf_getblock finds a lock that would block it: when F_WAIT is clear and lf_async_task is NULL it frees lock with lf_free_lock and returns EAGAIN; otherwise, for an F_FLOCK F_WRLCK request it first activates an F_UNLCK over the owner's own range (dropping shared locks it holds) and restores the type; then it adds outgoing wait edges with lf_add_outgoing under lf_owner_graph_lock, and if that returns an error (deadlock) it frees lock and returns that error. It inserts lock on state->ls_pending. If F_WAIT is clear (async request) it stores lock in *cookiep and returns EINPROGRESS, leaving lock on ls_pending owned by the lockf state (the caller must not free it). Otherwise it takes an extra reference, sleeps in sx_sleep on state->ls_lock (signal stops deferred), and then drops the sleep reference with lf_free_lock: if that was the last reference (the lock was freed) it returns EDOOFUS. If F_INTR is set in lock->lf_flags (set by lf_purgelocks) it returns EINTR after another lf_free_lock(lock). If lf_outedges is empty it returns 0 (the sleep error is ignored) with the lock active; if lf_outedges is not empty it calls lf_cancel_lock(state, lock), which removes it from the pending list, removes its graph edges and frees it, and the return value is the value returned by sx_sleep (0 or an errno). If nothing blocks, it adds incoming edges with lf_add_incoming; on error it frees lock and returns that error; otherwise it activates the lock with lf_activate_lock (an F_UNLCK request is an unlock and the entry is not left on the active list as a lock) and returns 0. state->ls_lock must be held by the caller (sx_sleep releases it while sleeping).
note: Three reviewer claims: (1) EINPROGRESS leaves lock on ls_pending, ownership not the caller's: right, and the rewritten prose states it (kern_lockf.c 1433-1453). (2) EDOOFUS path frees lock after the sleep, not while sleeping: right (1456-1463). (3) 'EINTR whenever F_INTR set, not only from lf_purgelocks, and this path does not remove edges': mostly WRONG, F_INTR is only set in lf_purgelocks (kern_lockf.c 796), which removes the edges itself (785-786); the check at 1486 only reports it.

name: loginclass_racct_foreach
prose: loginclass_racct_foreach(callback, pre, post, arg2, arg3) takes loginclasses_lock for reading, calls pre() if pre is not NULL, then walks the loginclasses list and calls callback(lc->lc_racct, arg2, arg3) once for each entry (callback is called without a NULL check), calls post() if post is not NULL, and releases the read lock. pre, the callbacks and post all run while the read lock is held. It returns no value and takes or drops no references.
note: slice cut the head: the function is loginclass_racct_foreach(callback, pre, post, arg2, arg3) (kern_loginclass.c 248-263), not loginclass_foreach. Old prose was otherwise accurate except it described the callback's first argument loosely and listed preconditions that are not in the code.

name: hardpps
prose: hardpps(tsp, delta_nsec) takes NTP_LOCK on entry and releases it at label out, the only exit (void). It always starts by setting STA_PPSSIGNAL and STA_PPSJITTER, clearing STA_PPSWANDER and STA_PPSERROR, and setting pps_valid = PPS_VALID. It rounds tsp to the nearest second into u_sec/u_nsec. If the new second equals pps_tf[0].tv_sec and the difference to pps_tf[0].tv_nsec is below NANOSECOND - MAXFREQ it goes to out without further changes. Otherwise it shifts the pps_tf[] samples and stores the new one, adds delta_nsec - NANOSECOND to pps_fcount, and if the difference to the previous sample is outside +-MAXFREQ it goes to out (STA_PPSJITTER stays set). Otherwise it clears STA_PPSJITTER, computes the median (v_nsec) and spread (u_nsec) of the three samples, and if the spread exceeds the popcorn threshold it sets STA_PPSJITTER and increments pps_jitcnt, else if STA_PPSTIME is set it sets time_monitor = -median and sets time_offset from it (no exit in either case). It then updates pps_jitter and, if fewer than (1 << pps_shift) seconds have passed since pps_lastsec, goes to out. At the end of a calibration interval it increments pps_calcnt, sets pps_lastsec, clears pps_fcount, and if the frequency error is beyond the limit or the interval length is not exactly 1 << pps_shift it sets STA_PPSERROR, increments pps_errcnt and goes to out. Otherwise it computes the frequency offset, adjusts pps_intcnt, STA_PPSWANDER and pps_stbcnt, adjusts pps_shift (within PPS_FAVG..pps_shiftmax), updates pps_stabil and pps_freq clamped to +-MAXFREQ, and copies pps_freq into time_freq if STA_PPSFREQ is set.
note: Reviewer claim is right: the popcorn-threshold and median-filter stages do not goto out (kern_ntptime.c 794-839), and early exits skip many of the listed updates. Old prose rewritten stage by stage (function is built under PPS_SYNC, kern_ntptime.c 743-926).

name: stop_all_proc
prose: stop_all_proc() (void) first calls stop_all_proc_block(), an interruptible exclusive acquisition of stop_all_proc_blocker; if that fails it returns at once without stopping anything and without holding the blocker. Otherwise it repeats passes over the allproc list, moving curproc along it. In each pass it skips processes with P_KPROC, P_SYSTEM, P_TOTAL_STOP or P_STOPPED_SIG set; it notes (seen_exiting) and skips processes with P2_WEXIT set; it notes (seen_stopped) and skips those with P_SHOULDSTOP equal to P_STOPPED_SINGLE; it skips traced processes (P_TRACED) without requesting a restart; for every other process it drops allproc_lock, holds the process, calls thread_single(p, SINGLE_ALLPROC), records restart if that returns non-zero or stopped_some if it returns zero, then releases the process and retakes the lock. After the pass it sets restart if allproc_gen changed. If any of restart, stopped_some, seen_exiting or seen_stopped is set it calls kern_yield(PRI_USER) and starts another pass; it returns when a whole pass sets none of them. On return the blocker is still held exclusively; the caller releases it through resume_all_proc / stop_all_proc_unblock.
note: Reviewer 3 is right (thread_single failure sets restart, kern_proc.c 3509-3510); reviewers 1 and 2 are also right that the early return when the blocker cannot be taken and the P_STOPPED_SIG skip are missing from the old prose, and the old statement that traced processes trigger a restart was wrong (3496-3505: they are skipped). Function is kern_proc.c 3450-3525.

name: tdsigwakeup
prose: tdsigwakeup(td, sig, action, intrval) is static and returns void; the caller holds the proc lock of td->td_proc. It takes the process spin lock (PROC_SLOCK) and the thread lock. If action is SIG_DFL, the signal has SIGPROP_KILL, td->td_priority is above PUSER and the thread is not an idle thread, it sets the thread priority to PUSER. If the thread is on a sleep queue: when the sleep is not interruptible (TDF_SINTR clear) it goes to out; if the signal has SIGPROP_CONT and action is SIG_DFL it releases the thread and process spin locks, deletes the signal from p->p_sigqueue and td->td_sigqueue and returns without waking the thread; if the signal has SIGPROP_STOP and TDF_SBDRY is set with TDF_SERESTART and TDF_SEINTR clear it goes to out; otherwise it raises a thread above PUSER (not idle) to PUSER, calls sig_sleepq_abort(td, intrval) (which releases the thread lock itself when intrval is 0 and TDF_SIGWAIT is not set, and otherwise calls sleepq_abort), releases the process spin lock and returns. If the thread is not on a sleep queue, on SMP it calls forward_signal(td) when the thread is running and is not curthread, and falls to out. At out it releases the process spin lock and then the thread lock.
note: Reviewers (in the history) are right: the sleep-abort path also raises a low priority thread to PUSER regardless of action (kern_sig.c 2679-2680), and the not-on-sleepq case can still have had the earlier SIGPROP_KILL priority raise (2639-2641). Old prose also said the thread lock is released inside sig_sleepq_abort on that path; that is only so when intrval is 0 and TDF_SIGWAIT is clear, otherwise sleepq_abort is called with the lock held (2330-2333).

name: sysctl_sysctl_next_node
prose: sysctl_sysctl_next_node(oidp, name, namelen, honor_skip) is static, reads only oidp->oid_kind, oid_number and oid_handler, reads name[0] only when namelen > 0 (name may be NULL when namelen is 0), writes nothing and takes no locks. It returns exactly one of ITER_SIBLINGS, ITER_FOUND or ITER_CHILDREN, in this order of tests: ITER_SIBLINGS if CTLFLAG_DORMANT is set, or if honor_skip is true and CTLFLAG_SKIP is set. If namelen == 0: ITER_FOUND if honor_skip is false, or the oid is not a CTLTYPE_NODE, or it has a non-NULL oid_handler; otherwise ITER_CHILDREN. If namelen > 0: ITER_SIBLINGS if oid_number < name[0]; if oid_number > name[0], ITER_FOUND if honor_skip is false, or the oid is not a node, or it has a handler, otherwise ITER_CHILDREN; if oid_number == name[0], ITER_SIBLINGS when the oid is not a node or has a handler, otherwise ITER_CHILDREN.
note: Reviewer claim (namelen==0 leaf/handler gives ITER_FOUND, not ITER_SIBLINGS) is WRONG about the old prose: the old prose already lists ITER_FOUND for namelen == 0 in those cases and ITER_SIBLINGS only for namelen > 0 (kern_sysctl.c 1267-1286). Old prose kept in substance; rewritten in code order (1256-1330).

name: kern_thr_suspend
prose: kern_thr_suspend(td, tsp) (td is the calling thread). If TDP_WAKEUP is set in td->td_pflags it clears it and returns 0 without taking the proc lock. Otherwise, if tsp is non-NULL: a zero timespec (tv_sec == 0 and tv_nsec == 0) sets error = EWOULDBLOCK and skips sleeping, and a non-zero one is converted with tvtohz into a tick timeout timo. It takes the proc lock; if no error is set and TDF_THRWAKEUP is not set it calls msleep on td with PCATCH and timo. If TDF_THRWAKEUP is then set (including when it was already set) it clears it under the thread lock, releases the proc lock and returns 0, whatever error was set before. Otherwise it releases the proc lock and returns: ETIMEDOUT if error is EWOULDBLOCK (zero timespec or sleep timeout); if msleep returned ERESTART, EINTR when timo is non-zero and ERESTART when timo is zero; otherwise the value returned by msleep (0 for a wakeup without TDF_THRWAKEUP, or another error such as EINTR from a signal).
note: Reviewer 2's claims are right on the first point (the TDP_WAKEUP path returns without the proc lock, kern_thr.c 547-550) and on the zero-timespec/THRWAKEUP point (566-572 return 0 first). Old prose already stated both; rewritten to follow the code and to add that other msleep results are passed through.

name: _callout_stop_safe
prose: _callout_stop_safe(c, flags) is the common callout stop/drain routine. Locking requirement: unless CS_DRAIN is set, if c->c_lock is Giant the caller's holding of Giant is only noted (use_lock = mtx_owned(&Giant)); if c->c_lock is another lock, the caller must hold it exclusively (lc_assert LA_XLOCKED); with CS_DRAIN the caller must be able to sleep and c_lock is not asserted. It takes the callout CPU lock (callout_lock), repeating the locking when the callout migrated. If the callout is not running (not cc_exec_curr) the initial result is 1; if it is running: without CS_DRAIN it clears CALLOUT_ACTIVE and returns 1 when use_lock is true and the execution is not already marked cancelled (it marks cc_exec_cancel and clears a pending deferred migration), or returns 0 when only a deferred migration is pending (the migration is cancelled, the running invocation is not stopped); otherwise the initial result is 0. With CS_DRAIN and the callout running, it takes the sleepqueue chain lock, drops the CPU lock (and Giant), sleeps on cc_exec_waiting until the invocation finishes, then restarts from the top. After that, if CALLOUT_PENDING is not set it returns -1 when the callout is not executing, or 0 when it still is; if pending, it clears CALLOUT_PENDING and CALLOUT_ACTIVE and removes the callout from the wheel or the expire queue (unless the special migration case marked it as not on a list), and returns the initial result (1 if it was not running, 0 if it was running). In the special case where CALLOUT_DFRMIGRATION and CALLOUT_PENDING and CALLOUT_ACTIVE were all set, it clears CALLOUT_PENDING and CALLOUT_ACTIVE and treats the callout as not on a list, so such a callout is reported as -1 (or 0 if it is executing). Every return path releases the callout CPU lock; the sleepqueue chain lock is released before returning, and the caller's own c_lock is not released.
note: Reviewer 2 is right that -1 is returned for a callout that is neither pending nor executing (kern_timeout.c 1301-1311) and the old prose said this too; the old prose however wrongly said the CALLOUT_DFRMIGRATION race case returns 1: after it clears CALLOUT_PENDING (1138) the code reaches the not-pending branch and returns -1 (0 if the callout is also executing). Reviewer 1 (Giant need not be held) is right and already reflected. Rewritten from kern_timeout.c 1087-1330.

name: coredump
prose: coredump(td, errmsg) is entered with the proc lock of td->td_proc held (asserted) and td single-threaded in the process if it has several threads (MPASS). It returns EFAULT, after releasing the proc lock and storing a message in *errmsg, if kern.coredump is off, the process has P2_NOTRACE set, or the process is P_SUGID and kern.sugid_coredump is off. It returns EFBIG, after releasing the proc lock and setting *errmsg, if RLIMIT_CORE is 0 or racct_get_available(RACCT_CORE) is 0. Otherwise, under the coredump rmlock held for reading, it goes through the registered coredumpers: an entry without a probe is chosen as COREDUMPER_GENERIC priority if nothing has been chosen yet; for the others cd_probe(td) is called, a negative result skips the entry and a result above the best priority so far makes it the chosen one. It takes a reference on the chosen coredumper's cd_refcount (blockcount_acquire), drops the rmlock, calls the chosen cd_handle(td, limit), asserts that the proc lock is not held afterwards (the handler is expected to release it), drops the reference and returns the handler's return value. If no coredumper is registered, chosen is NULL (the MPASS that expects the built-in vnode dumper comes after the refcount acquire).
note: slice cut the head: the function is the static coredump(td, errmsg) (kern_ucoredump.c 221-308), not coredump_select_and_handle. Old prose wrongly said the caller must not hold the proc lock; coredump asserts it is held on entry (line 230).

name: link_elf_load_file
prose: link_elf_load_file(cls, filename, result) loads a relocatable (ET_REL) ELF kernel module. It opens filename with vn_open, returning that error directly if the open fails; every later exit goes through label out, which unlocks and closes the vnode, frees the nameidata, calls linker_file_unload(lf, LINKER_UNLOAD_FORCE) if an error is set and a linker file was created, frees the ELF header buffer, and returns error. The error values set before out are: ENOEXEC for a non-regular file, a short or failed header read, a non-ELF or unsupported class, data layout, version or machine, a bad section header table, no loadable sections, not exactly one symbol table, invalid symbol strings, a missing symbol table, or a count mismatch of the loaded progbits, rel or rela tables; ENOSYS if the type is not ET_REL; ENOMEM if linker_make_file, vm_pager_allocate, vm_map_find or vm_map_wire fails or if the final mapbase does not equal address + mapsize; EINVAL for a short read of the symbol table, string tables, section contents or relocation tables; ENOSPC if the section's address pointer is NULL (a failed DPCPU/VNET allocation); the errors from MAC (mac_kld_check_load), link_elf_detect_insecure_early and _late, vn_rdwr, link_elf_reloc_local, linker_load_dependencies, relocate_file and elf_cpu_load_file. On success it maps and wires a single region, loads or zeroes every allocatable PROGBITS, NOBITS, INIT_ARRAY, FINI_ARRAY (and amd64 UNWIND) section, rebases the symbol values, reads the relocation tables, applies local, external and (on i386 and amd64) ifunc relocations, calls link_elf_protect and link_elf_invoke_ctors, stores lf in *result and returns 0.
note: slice cut the head: the function is link_elf_load_file(cls, filename, result) (link_elf_obj.c 770-1346), not elf_obj_load. The old prose wrongly assumed lf, ef and the headers were already read and validated by the caller; this function opens and parses the file itself.

name: bioq_disksort
prose: bioq_disksort(head, bp) inserts bp into head->queue and returns nothing; it takes no lock and its callers must serialise access to head. Using bioq_insert_tail (bp becomes the last element, head->total is incremented, head->batched is set to 0, head->insert_point and head->last_offset are set to bp and bp->bio_offset) when BIO_ORDERED is set in bp->bio_flags, or bp->bio_cmd is none of BIO_READ, BIO_WRITE and BIO_DELETE, or bioq_batchsize > 0 and head->batched > bioq_batchsize. Otherwise it does a sorted insertion: with key(x) = (uoff_t)(x->bio_offset - head->last_offset), it starts at the first element, or at the element after head->insert_point if insert_point is set, skips elements whose key is <= the key of bp, and inserts bp after the last skipped element, or at the head of the queue if none was skipped and insert_point is NULL; head->total and head->batched are each incremented by one and insert_point and last_offset are not changed.
note: No reviewer disagreement in packet (only mechanical rejections); I re-read the function (subr_disk.c 246-299) and the prose matches the code. Kept, with 'never fails' qualified.

name: intrcnt_updatename
prose: intrcnt_updatename(isrc) (static) calls mtx_assert(&isrc_table_lock, MA_OWNED) (only effective when assertions are compiled in) and then intrcnt_setname(isrc->isrc_event->ie_fullname, isrc->isrc_index), which does snprintf into the INTRNAME_LEN-byte slot at intrnames + INTRNAME_LEN * index with format '%-*s' and width INTRNAME_LEN - 1. The slot therefore holds ie_fullname left-justified and padded with spaces to INTRNAME_LEN - 1 characters, then a NUL; a name longer than INTRNAME_LEN - 1 characters is truncated to its first INTRNAME_LEN - 1 characters. The stored string equals ie_fullname exactly only when strlen(ie_fullname) is exactly INTRNAME_LEN - 1. It returns nothing and takes, drops and allocates nothing.
note: Reviewers 2 and 3 are right in part: the slot equals ie_fullname only when its length is exactly INTRNAME_LEN - 1, shorter names are space-padded (subr_intr.c 228-229, 241), longer ones are cut by snprintf's size INTRNAME_LEN. Reviewer 2's 'also exactly INTRNAME_LEN-1' is the only equality case. Old prose was wrong on 'equals exactly when <=' and on the padding.

name: kdb_trap
prose: kdb_trap(type, code, tf) returns 0 at once, with no other effect, if kdb_dbbe is NULL or its dbbe_trap is NULL, or if kdb_active is already non-zero. Otherwise it disables interrupts (intr_disable). If the scheduler is not already stopped it (on SMP) stops the other CPUs that are not in stopped_cpus with stop_cpus_hard, sets scheduler_stopped to true and remembers that it did so (did_stop_cpus). It increments kdb_active, sets kdb_frame to tf, calls kdb_cpu_trap, makectx and kdb_thr_select(curthread), and grabs the console (cngrab). In a loop it checks kdb_backend_permitted for the current back-end; if it is not permitted it sets handled = 1 and leaves the loop; otherwise it calls be->dbbe_trap(type, code) and stores the result in handled. If kdb_dbbe is still the same back-end it leaves the loop; if the back-end changed it switches to the new one and loops, leaving the loop if the new one is NULL or has no dbbe_trap. It then calls cnungrab, decrements kdb_active, and only if it stopped the CPUs itself it clears scheduler_stopped and restarts the CPUs it had stopped (on SMP); finally it restores the interrupt state and returns handled, which is the last value set in the loop.
note: Reviewer claim (scheduler_stopped cleared only when did_stop_cpus is set) is right: kdb_trap clears it and restarts CPUs only inside 'if (did_stop_cpus)' (subr_kdb.c 803-809). Old prose also implied the loop 'on every path' decrements kdb_active, which is true, but the CPU restart/scheduler flag part was overstated.

name: memdesc_alloc_ext_mbufs
prose: memdesc_alloc_ext_mbufs(mem, ext_alloc, extpg_alloc, cb_arg, how, offset, len, actual_len, can_truncate) builds an mbuf chain for the byte range [offset, offset + len) of the memory descriptor mem by calling a helper chosen by mem->md_type: vaddr_ext_mbuf (MEMDESC_VADDR), paddr_ext_mbuf (PADDR), vlist_ext_mbuf (VLIST), plist_ext_mbuf (PLIST), mbuf_subchain (MBUF), vmpages_ext_mbuf (VMPAGES); MEMDESC_UIO panics with 'uio not supported' and any other type reaches __assert_unreachable. If the helper returns NULL it returns NULL without writing *actual_len. Otherwise it asserts (KASSERT, only when INVARIANTS is on) that the length done is at most len when can_truncate is true and exactly len when it is false, and that m_length of the chain equals done; if actual_len is non-NULL it stores done there; it returns the chain.
note: slice cut the head: the slice (subr_memdesc.c 790-799) is the tail of memdesc_alloc_ext_mbufs(mem, ext_alloc, extpg_alloc, cb_arg, how, offset, len, actual_len, can_truncate) (748-799). Old prose omitted the NULL return and the dispatch on md_type.

name: _MSAN_ATOMIC_FUNC_LOAD(name, type)
prose: Generated function kmsan_atomic_load_<name>(ptr) (from _MSAN_ATOMIC_FUNC_LOAD) calls kmsan_check_arg(sizeof(ptr)) and kmsan_shadow_check on the sizeof(type) bytes at ptr (both report an uninitialized value but do not stop the load), calls kmsan_init_ret(sizeof(type)) to mark the return value initialized, and returns atomic_load_<name>(ptr). Generated function kmsan_atomic_store_<name>(ptr, val) (from _MSAN_ATOMIC_FUNC_STORE, returns void) calls kmsan_check_arg(sizeof(ptr) + sizeof(val)), fills the shadow of the sizeof(type) bytes at ptr with KMSAN_STATE_INITED, then calls atomic_store_<name>(ptr, val). Neither allocates memory or takes a lock.
note: macro-generated: the packet item is the macro families _MSAN_ATOMIC_FUNC_LOAD / MSAN_ATOMIC_FUNC_LOAD and _MSAN_ATOMIC_FUNC_STORE / MSAN_ATOMIC_FUNC_STORE (subr_msan.c 1240-1267), expanded for bool, 8, 16, 32, 64, char, short, int, long and ptr (the non-underscore macros also generate the acq_ load and rel_ store variants). Old prose omitted the shadow check of the load and the argument checks.

name: MSAN_ATOMIC_FUNC_TESTANDSET(name, type)
prose: Generated functions of the form kmsan_atomic_<op>_<name>(...) for <op> in fetchadd, readandclear, testandset and swap. Each first calls kmsan_check_arg on the sizes of its arguments, then kmsan_shadow_check on the sizeof(type) bytes at ptr, then kmsan_init_ret for the size of its return type, and returns the value of the corresponding atomic_<op>_<name> routine, so the memory operation itself is done by that routine. kmsan_atomic_fetchadd_<name>(ptr, val), kmsan_atomic_readandclear_<name>(ptr) and kmsan_atomic_swap_<name>(ptr, val) return type; kmsan_atomic_testandset_<name>(ptr, v) takes a u_int v and returns int. The checks only report uninitialized arguments or memory; they do not change the result.
note: macro-generated: the packet item covers four macro families, MSAN_ATOMIC_FUNC_FETCHADD, READANDCLEAR, TESTANDSET and SWAP (subr_msan.c 1145-1198), expanded for the widths listed in 1301-1329. Old prose said testandset returns the old value, but its generated function returns int from atomic_testandset_<name>(ptr, v) and takes a u_int bit argument.

name: kvprintf
prose: kvprintf(fmt, func, arg, radix, ap) formats into either func(c, arg) per character (when func is non-NULL) or, when func is NULL, into the buffer at arg, with no terminating NUL stored. It returns the number of characters emitted, and its only return is when the format scan reaches the NUL terminator of fmt. A NULL fmt is replaced by '(fmt null)\n'; a radix below 2 or above 36 is replaced by 10. Plain characters are copied. Conversions handled: flags and widths (# + - 0, digits, *, .), length modifiers (h hh l ll q j t z), % (literal), b (value plus a bit-name string, printed as number then <names>), c, D (hex dump of a byte pointer with a separator string, width default 16), d i u o x X y p r, s (NULL string printed as '(null)', precision limits length), and n (argument consumed, nothing stored). After a conversion letter the output is padded to width as requested. If the letter after '%' and its flags is not one of those, the default case emits the text from the '%' through that character literally, consumes no argument, and sets stop, after which all remaining fmt text is emitted literally (including any '%') up to the terminating NUL. A '%' as the last character before the NUL goes through the default case, which emits the '%' and the NUL character and then continues to read fmt beyond the terminator. When func is NULL the caller's buffer must be large enough for every emitted character.
note: Reviewer claim (default case copies only the invalid specifier and stops; does not copy the remaining text) is WRONG: the default case sets stop = 1 (subr_prf.c 1051) and the outer while loop at line 753 tests 'ch != '%' || stop', so with stop set every remaining format character, including further '%', is emitted literally. The old prose is right on that point. Added the NUL-terminated edge case and %b/%D details; function is subr_prf.c 721-1056.

name: vsscanf
prose: vsscanf(inp, fmt0, ap) scans the NUL-terminated string inp (inr is set to strlen(inp)) according to fmt0 and stores the converted values through pointer arguments from ap. A format white space character skips input white space; any other non-% format character must equal the next input character (end of input: input_failure, mismatch: match_failure). Supported conversions are %% (literal), the modifiers * (suppress), h, hh, l, ll, q, j, t, z and a decimal width, and d, i, o, u, x, p (integers via strtoq or strtouq on a bounded copy in buf), s, c, [ (character class built by __sccl) and n (stores the number of characters consumed so far, counts as a conversion, does not need input). Conversions other than n need non-empty remaining input (otherwise input_failure) and skip leading white space except for %c and %[ . %c without suppression copies width bytes with bcopy without comparing width to the remaining input length. A conversion letter not listed matches no case in either switch, so it assigns nothing and consumes no argument. The returns are: at the end of fmt0, nassigned (the number of assigned fields); input_failure returns nassigned if at least one conversion has been counted, otherwise -1; match_failure returns nassigned. It takes no locks and allocates nothing.
note: slice cut the head and is the middle of vsscanf(inp, fmt0, ap) (subr_scanf.c 97-562); there is no function named vfscanf in this file. Old prose described variables that do not exist (inp/inr is a NUL-terminated string here, inr is strlen(inp)).

name: stats_v1_vsd_tdgst_add
prose: stats_v1_vsd_tdgst_add(vs_dtype, tdgst, x, weight, attempt) (static inline) adds a weighted sample x to the t-digest tdgst. It returns EOVERFLOW if smplcnt + weight would overflow the 32-bit or 64-bit counter, and EINVAL if vs_dtype is neither VSD_DTYPE_TDGSTCLUST32 nor VSD_DTYPE_TDGSTCLUST64; both are returned before the tree is touched. In a loop it returns EAGAIN if attempt >= 5, scans the centroids in order to find those nearest to x, and, for centroids around that position, computes a size limit k from the quantile; a centroid is a merge candidate when its cnt + weight does not exceed k, and one candidate is chosen at random with random(). Q-type arithmetic errors in this step are returned. If no candidate is found and the tree is full (ARB_FULL), it calls stats_v1_vsd_tdgst_compress with attempt (and then increments attempt) and repeats the search; an error from the compression is returned. If a candidate was found it subtracts the centroid mean from x, divides by cnt + weight (an ERANGE from the division is ignored), adds the result to the mean, increases cnt by weight and reinserts the centroid; any other Q-type error is returned before cnt or smplcnt change; reinsertion returning a node gives EALREADY. If no candidate was found it takes a free centroid with ARB_GETFREE (EAGAIN if none), sets mu to x and cnt to weight (for 32 bit via Q_QCPYVALQ, whose error is returned), and inserts it (EALREADY if the insert reports a duplicate). After a merge or insert that got that far, smplcnt is increased by weight, in the EALREADY cases too, and the function returns the error value (0 on success).
note: slice cut the head and was a middle fragment of stats_v1_vsd_tdgst_add(vs_dtype, tdgst, x, weight, attempt) (subr_stats.c 3083-3453); there is no function stats_v1_vsd_tdgst_update (the update wrapper is stats_v1_voi_update_tdgst at 3455). Old prose omitted the early errors, the retry loop and the EALREADY result.

name: syscallret
prose: syscallret(td) is the common end-of-syscall path for a thread (void). If td_errno is ENOTCAPABLE or ECAPMODE, the thread is in capability mode and either trap_enotcap or P2_TRAPCAP is set, it (with PAX_SEGVGUARD, notes the segfault and) sends the thread a SIGTRAP with code TRAP_CAP through trapsignal. It then calls userret, and under KTRACE records a KTR_SYSRET event when the trace point is active. If the process is traced it sets TDB_SCX in td_dbgflags under the proc lock. If the process is traced or td_dbgflags has TDB_EXEC or TDB_FORK, it takes the proc lock and: for a traced process with TDB_EXEC set and a parent whose ABI is Linux it raises a ptrace stop (ptracestop, SIGTRAP) and clears TDB_EXEC; for a traced process with TDB_FORK or TDB_EXEC set, or with PTRACE_SCX in p_ptevents, it sets TDB_BOUNDARY and raises a ptrace stop; then it clears TDB_SCX, TDB_EXEC, TDB_FORK and TDB_BOUNDARY and releases the proc lock. Otherwise (not traced and neither flag set) td_dbgflags is not changed and no ptrace stop is taken.
note: slice cut the head: the function is the static inline syscallret(td) (subr_syscall.c 219-304), not syscall_exit. The old prose listed only part of the effect and wrongly implied TDB_SCX is always cleared.

name: taskqueue_enqueue_timeout_sbt
prose: taskqueue_enqueue_timeout_sbt(queue, timeout_task, sbt, pr, flags) takes the queue lock (TQ_LOCK), asserts (KASSERT) that timeout_task->q is NULL or queue, sets timeout_task->q = queue, and records res = the current timeout_task->t.ta_pending. It releases the queue lock on every path and returns res or -1. If DT_DRAIN_IN_PROGRESS is set in timeout_task->f it unlocks and returns -1, doing nothing else. Otherwise if sbt == 0 it calls taskqueue_enqueue_locked(queue, &timeout_task->t, 0) (which releases the lock; its return value is ignored) and returns res. Otherwise, if DT_CALLOUT_ARMED is already set it increments res; if it is not set it increments queue->tq_callouts, sets DT_CALLOUT_ARMED and negates a negative sbt. Then, only if sbt is greater than 0 (after that possible negation) it resets the callout: for a spin queue (tq_spin) it adds C_DIRECT_EXEC to flags; if the queue is a spin queue with tq_tcount == 1 and its only thread is curthread it uses callout_reset_sbt_curcpu, otherwise callout_reset_sbt, in both cases with sbt, pr, taskqueue_timeout_func and the timeout task. It then unlocks the queue and returns res. So with a negative sbt and the callout already armed the callout is neither reset nor cancelled.
note: Reviewer claims all right: (1) the lock is also released on the drain-in-progress path (subr_taskqueue.c 347-350); (2) in the armed case a negative sbt is not negated and is not used to reset the callout, and in the unarmed case it is negated before the reset (360-363), so the old prose's 'reset only when sbt > 0 in the armed case' was misleading; (3) C_DIRECT_EXEC is added for any spin queue when sbt > 0 (364-365), the curcpu reset is used only for a spin queue with exactly one thread which is curthread (366-367). Rewritten from lines 336-378.

name: pipe_direct_write
prose: pipe_direct_write(wpipe, uio) is called with the pipe mutex and the pipe lock held (pipelock/pipeunlock are used around its sleeps, and it returns with them held). At retry it returns EPIPE through error1 if PIPE_EOF is set. If PIPE_DIRECTW is set (another direct write in progress) or if the pipe buffer is non-empty, it wakes a waiting reader and select, sets PIPE_WANTW, sleeps in msleep (interruptible); an msleep error is returned through error1 and PIPE_DIRECTW is left as it was; otherwise it retries from the top. Otherwise it calls pipe_build_write_buffer, which maps at most one chunk (the smaller of the first iovec's length and the pipe buffer size), reduces uio_resid, iov_len and uio_offset by that size and returns EFAULT if the user pages cannot be held; an error is returned through error1 with nothing mapped. It then sleeps (interruptibly) until the reader consumes the mapped data (pipe_pages.cnt becomes 0) or PIPE_EOF is set, waking readers and select before each sleep. After the loop: if PIPE_EOF is set it zeroes pipe_pages.cnt, destroys the write buffer, calls pipeselwakeup and returns EPIPE (the mapped chunk already counted in uio_resid is lost); else if the last msleep returned EINTR or ERESTART it copies the unread part of the mapped data into the pipe buffer with pipe_clone_write_buffer and returns that error; otherwise it destroys the write buffer and returns 0. wakeup(wpipe) is called only on the error1 exits (EPIPE at entry, an msleep error in the two waits before mapping, or a failure of pipe_build_write_buffer), not on the three exits after the mapping.
note: Reviewer claims: (a) 'only one chunk is mapped, not all of the remaining data' right (sys_pipe.c 961-988, the chunk is at most min(first iov length, pipe buffer size)); (b) 'PIPE_DIRECTW remains set on EINTR while waiting for another direct write' right, this path returns via error1 without touching it (1069-1081); (c) 'EINTR/ERESTART path and EPIPE-after-mapping path return without wakeup(wpipe)' right: only the paths that go to error1 call wakeup (1135-1137). Old prose said the error from the build call could be ENOMEM, but pipe_build_write_buffer returns EFAULT only.

name: pipe_write
prose: pipe_write(fp, uio, active_cred, flags, td) writes uio to the pipe whose read-side pipe is fp->f_data. It takes the mutex of rpipe and calls pipelock(wpipe, true); if that fails it unlocks the mutex and returns its error. It returns EPIPE (both locks released) if wpipe->pipe_present is not PIPE_ACTIVE or PIPE_EOF is set, and, under MAC, the error of mac_pipe_check_write (both locks released). Otherwise it increments pipe_busy, may choose a larger or smaller buffer size and call pipespace (its result is not checked), and loops while uio_resid is non-zero: it breaks with EPIPE if PIPE_EOF appears; for a user-space write whose first iovec length and buffer size are at least pipe_mindirect on a blocking file it calls pipe_direct_write and breaks on its error; if a direct write's pages are pending (pipe_pages.cnt != 0) it waits in an interruptible msleep (an msleep error breaks the loop); otherwise it copies as much as fits into the circular buffer with uiomove (writes of at most PIPE_BUF bytes are not started unless all of them fit), breaking on a uiomove error; if there is no space it wakes a waiting reader, breaks with EAGAIN when FNONBLOCK is set, otherwise wakes select, sets PIPE_WANTW and sleeps interruptibly (an msleep error breaks the loop). After the loop it decrements pipe_busy; if pipe_busy is 0 and PIPE_WANT is set it clears PIPE_WANT and PIPE_WANTR and wakes the pipe; otherwise, if the buffer holds data and PIPE_WANTR is set, it clears PIPE_WANTR and wakes the reader. If some bytes were consumed from uio and the error is EPIPE the error becomes 0; if error is 0 the pipe mtime is updated; select is woken if the buffer is non-empty; both locks are released; ru_msgsnd is incremented if any bytes were transferred; the function returns error (EPIPE, EAGAIN, EFAULT or another uiomove error, an msleep error, an error from pipe_direct_write, or 0).
note: Reviewer claim (pipe_busy reaching zero clears the flags and wakes only when PIPE_WANT is set) is right (sys_pipe.c 1363-1377): with PIPE_WANT clear the code falls to the else-if branch that only wakes a reader (and clears PIPE_WANTR) when data is buffered. Function is the static pipe_write(fp, uio, active_cred, flags, td), sys_pipe.c 1141-1403.

name: kern_ptrace
prose: kern_ptrace(td, req, pid, addr, data) performs one ptrace request on process pid (or on the process owning thread id pid when pid > PID_MAX). For most requests (PT_TRACE_ME, PT_ATTACH, PT_STEP, PT_CONTINUE, PT_TO_SCE, PT_TO_SCX, PT_SYSCALL, PT_FOLLOW_FORK, PT_LWP_EVENTS, PT_GET_EVENT_MASK, PT_SET_EVENT_MASK, PT_DETACH, PT_GET_SC_ARGS) it first takes proctree_lock exclusively. It returns ESRCH at once (unlocking proctree_lock if taken) if the process or thread is not found; otherwise it holds the target's proc lock and returns, through the common exit, with that lock released and proctree_lock released if still held. Early failures (go to fail) are ESRCH when P_WEXIT is set, errors of p_cansee and p_candebug, EINVAL for a system process, EPERM under PAX capsicum restrictions, and per request: PT_TRACE_ME gives EBUSY if already traced and EPERM if the parent is init; PT_ATTACH gives EINVAL for itself or an ancestor of a traced caller, EBUSY if already traced; other requests (except PT_CLEARSTEP on the caller's own thread) give the error of proc_can_ptrace, and may sleep until P2_PTRACEREQ clears, returning an msleep error or ESRCH if the process changed. Then it sets P2_PTRACEREQ and holds the process, and performs the request: attach and trace-me mark the process traced and reparent/stop it; step, continue, to-syscall and detach return EINVAL for a signal outside 0.._SIG_MAXSIG or the error of ptrace_single_step or ptrace_set_pc, and detach undoes the tracing, reparents back and clears event state; kill, continue and the like then deliver the signal by clearing pending reports, setting p_xsig and unsuspending threads; read/write requests (PT_READ_*, PT_WRITE_*, PT_IO) give ENOMEM for a short word transfer, EINVAL for a bad PT_IO length or operation, or the error of proc_rwmem; register and register-set requests return the machine-dependent copy error; PT_LWPINFO, PT_GETNUMLWPS, PT_GETLWPLIST (EINVAL for a non-positive count, copyout error), PT_VM_TIMESTAMP and PT_VM_ENTRY report information; PT_GET_EVENT_MASK and PT_SET_EVENT_MASK need data equal to sizeof(int) and the latter rejects unknown bits (EINVAL); PT_GET_SC_ARGS/PTLINUX_GET_SC_ARGS and PT_GET_SC_RET need the thread to be at a syscall stop (EINVAL otherwise); PT_COREDUMP gives EINVAL for unknown flags, the error of fget_write, EPIPE for a non-regular file, the error of proc_can_ptrace, EBUSY if no thread can be selected, otherwise the core dump error; PT_SC_REMOTE gives EBUSY unless the thread is at a boundary stop, ESRCH if the thread left the process, and otherwise 0; machine-dependent requests are passed to cpu_ptrace when supported, and any other request gives EINVAL. At out the hold on the process is dropped (_PRELE); at fail P2_PTRACEREQ is cleared (with a wakeup) if this call set it, the proc lock is released, proctree_lock is released if still held and error is returned. td->td_retval[0] is set to 0 at the start and by some requests to a result (PT_READ_*, PT_GETNUMLWPS, PT_GETLWPLIST, PT_VM_TIMESTAMP).
note: slice cut the head and is the middle of kern_ptrace(td, req, pid, addr, data) (sys_process.c 937-1859); there is no function named ptrace_request. Old prose was a fragment and wrongly claimed no state is committed on failure (several requests change state before they can fail, and the failure cleanup at fail only drops flags).

name: systrace_return_setargdesc
prose: systrace_return_setargdesc(sysnum, ndx, desc, descsz) (static, generated, void) starts with p = NULL, selects the case for sysnum, and in each known case sets p to a return-type string (for example 'int' or 'ssize_t' or 'void') only when ndx is 0 or 1; case labels that have no body of their own share the assignment of the next case that has one. For an unknown sysnum, or any other ndx, p stays NULL. At the end, if p is not NULL it copies the string into desc with strlcpy(desc, p, descsz), otherwise desc is not written. It returns no value and takes no locks.

name: systrace_args
prose: systrace_args(sysnum, params, uarg, n_args) (static, generated, void) converts the argument structure params of system call sysnum into the register array uarg: with iarg being the same storage viewed as int64_t, for each case it reads the fields of the corresponding struct (params cast to that syscall's argument struct) and stores them in order into iarg[a++] (integer-typed arguments, sign-extended) or uarg[a++] (pointer and unsigned arguments, cast through intptr_t or copied), then stores the argument count in *n_args. System calls with no arguments set *n_args = 0 without reading params. The default case, for a sysnum with no case, sets *n_args = 0 and writes nothing to uarg. It returns no value.
note: slice cut the head and is the middle of the generated function systrace_args(sysnum, params, uarg, n_args) (systrace_args.c 9-3552), a switch over sysnum; it is not a separate unnamed function. Old prose assumed an argument struct matches the syscall number, which is the precondition, but it also omitted the default case.
